metadata.title: Within Physicalism | Part 2 What Culture Does Our Metaphysics Produce?
metadata.description:
Within Physicalism | Part 2
What Kind of Culture Does Our Metaphysics Produce?

If Part 1 explored how a dominant metaphysical framework becomes embedded within our institutions, Part 2 asks a different question:

What kind of culture emerges once that framework becomes the air we breathe?

This essay explores how particular physicalist traditions may shape the way we understand ourselves, nature, meaning, and society—not by arguing that Physicalism is false, but by asking whether any culturally dominant metaphysics leaves an imprint upon the civilisation that lives within it.

The aim is not to settle the debate between Physicalism, Idealism, Dual-Aspect Monism, or any other metaphysical position.

Instead, it asks a broader philosophical question:

When a metaphysical framework becomes culturally dominant, what kinds of assumptions, institutions, and ways of living tend to emerge alongside it?

If Part 1 examined how metaphysics becomes culture, Part 2 explores what life within that culture might look like.

I'd love to hear your thoughts in the comments. Please keep the discussion thoughtful and respectful, especially where we disagree. Philosophy advances through dialogue rather than victory.

metadata.title: Carl Jung on the Psychology of Timing — Why Some Ideas Land When They Do
metadata.description:
The same piece of advice can mean nothing to you at one point in your life, and feel completely different a few years later, even though the words haven't changed. Carl Jung had a real psychological explanation for why timing affects how ideas land — one rooted in readiness, not coincidence or fate.

This video looks at what Jung believed determines whether a person is actually able to hear something, versus simply encountering it. It covers the relationship between psychological readiness, the unconscious, and why certain ideas seem to "click" only once someone has already done a certain amount of internal groundwork, whether they were aware of doing it or not.

What we explore:

Why psychological readiness affects whether an idea genuinely lands, according to Jung's model. The role of the unconscious in preparing someone to receive an insight before they consciously recognize it. Why the same information can mean something completely different at different points in a person's life.

References & further reading:

Carl Jung — Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933); Psychology and Alchemy; Two Essays on Analytical Psychology.

A note on accuracy: This video presents Jung's ideas in accessible language for a general audience. For the full depth and nuance of his work, the original texts above go much further than any single video can.

#CarlJung #Psychology #PersonalGrowth #Individuation #SelfDevelopment

metadata.title: Ajahn Amaro – The spaciousness around thoughts is what frees the heart
metadata.description:
Here Ajahn Amaro reflects on how we designate value to experience and make it absolute, and how important awareness and spaciousness around that is in our practice.

This is an outtake from our retreat day with Ajahn Amaro in July 2026, looking at what the Buddha taught about the nature of true wisdom and its relationship to knowledge and to information.

_____________________________ 

AJAHN AMARO

Ajahn Amaro was born 1956 in England; he went to London University and graduated with a joint honours degree in psychology & physiology.

He was ordained as a monk by Ven. Ajahn Chah in April 1979. He trained in England from 1979 to 1995 under Ven. Ajahn Sumedho and started going to the USA to teach in 1990; in June 1996 he opened Abhayagiri Monastery, in Redwood Valley, California. He was co-abbot there, with Ajahn Pasanno, until 2010 when, on Ajahn Sumedho’s retirement, he took up the role of abbot at Amaravati Monastery, in Hertfordshire. 

He has authored or co-authored about 20 books on Buddhist themes. In 2015 he was honoured by the King of Thailand with the title Chao Khun Videsabuddhiguna.

metadata.title: A Breathscape Practice for Cultivating Mindfulness
metadata.description:
It is natural as finite human beings to want to feel certain. To our brains, certainty equals safety. It’s normal to wish we could control the future, because uncertainty can be unsettling and scary. 

 But as today’s teacher observes, as difficult as it is, the only real leverage we have to positively influence the future is to learn to inhabit the present moment fully, without trying to fix it or manage it. This is the most challenging aspect of mindfulness, and its core principle. 

 This 20-minute guided meditation with Jon Kabat-Zinn is practice for simply being awake and aware in the moment without agenda. 

 Jon Kabat-Zinn is the founder of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) as well as the Center for Mindfulness in Medicine, Health Care, and Society at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. He is author of  Full Catastrophe Living: Using the Wisdom of Your Body and Mind to Face Stress, Pain, and Illness;  Wherever You Go, There You Are;  Coming to Our Senses; and  Mindfulness for Beginners. He trains, teaches, and lectures throughout the world on applications of mindfulness and is Professor of Medicine Emeritus at the University of Massachusetts Medical School.

 The transcription of this guided meditation will be online and in our app at Mindful.org next week. 

 Stay curious, stay inspired. Sign up for our free newsletter mindful.org/signup or download the app for free at mindful.org/app. 

 Show Notes

 Find more from Jon Kabat Zinn here.

 Go Deeper

 Like any mindful skill, learning how to tune into and stay rooted in the present moment takes time and practice. Learn more with these resources on Mindful:

    The Science and Practice of Staying Present Through Difficult Times

✎ Successful entrepreneurs achieve extraordinary results by making calculated choices that average people actively avoid. High achievers like Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sarah Blakely, and Richard Branson built massive empires by adopting specific mental models that completely transform how they evaluate risk, handle failure, and solve complex problems. By breaking obstacles down to fundamental truths using first principles thinking rather than copying others, entrepreneurs can spot cheap, scalable solutions to massive challenges. Applying a regret minimization framework allows individuals to look at choices from the perspective of their eighty-year-old self, eliminating the fear of short-term rejection and making the right career decisions completely obvious. Additionally, focusing on asymmetric risk allows founders to take smart bets where the potential downside is minimal while the potential upside remains life-changing.

✎ Achieving extreme wealth requires building sustainable daily systems rather than simply setting ambitious goals. While goals provide a target, daily routines, habits, and systems are what actually drive long-term execution. High performers avoid the trap of survivorship bias by analyzing unseen fundamentals instead of blindly copying visible success stories. They also master the difficult skill of cutting losses quickly when a strategy fails, ruthlessly eliminating sunk costs to redirect resources toward better opportunities. Driven by a mission to serve others and solve major real-world problems, successful founders look past surface-level intelligence and overanalysis to focus entirely on consistent action, emotional intelligence, and building meaningful partnerships.

✎ Smart individuals often struggle to reach their full potential when they fall into common mental traps like overthinking, perfectionism, relying on natural talent over hard work, and living in theory instead of reality. Overcoming analysis paralysis requires setting strict decision deadlines and launching projects even when they feel imperfect, because real-world feedback is necessary to refine any product or business model. metadata.title: Jon Kabat-Zinn: A Breathscape Practice for Cultivating Mindfulness
metadata.description:
It is natural as finite human beings to want to feel certain. To our brains, certainty equals safety. It’s normal to wish we could control the future, because uncertainty can be unsettling and scary. 
 

But as today’s teacher observes, as difficult as it is, the only real leverage we have to positively influence the future is to learn to inhabit the present moment fully, without trying to fix it or manage it. This is the most challenging aspect of mindfulness, and its core principle. 
 

This 20-minute guided meditation with Jon Kabat-Zinn is practice for simply being awake and aware in the moment without agenda. 
 

Jon Kabat-Zinn is the founder of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) as well as the Center for Mindfulness in Medicine, Health Care, and Society (https://www.umassmed.edu/cfm/)  at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. metadata.title: You are Living in the Lowest Level of Reality
metadata.description:
Is physical reality actually real? Examine the philosophical nature of existence and why our perception of the world might be limited. This presentation explores the boundary between tangible experience and the abstract nature of the universe. By analyzing visual cues and cosmic imagery, we question the fundamental assumptions we make about the physical world. This is for anyone interested in metaphysics, perception theory, and the nature of consciousness. After watching, you will have a new framework to consider how your brain constructs the reality you live in every day. We look at why what we perceive as real might be a construct rather than an absolute truth. Understanding the limits of physical reality helps clarify how we interact with the space around us. It also raises a deeper question: if our senses only give us a limited representation of the world, then what exists beyond that representation? The reality we experience may feel complete simply because our brains are designed to make it feel complete. We rarely question the information coming through our senses because everything around us appears consistent, familiar, and tangible. But consistency does not necessarily mean completeness. Our perception is shaped by the limits of our senses, the structure of our brains, and the way information is interpreted before it ever reaches our conscious awareness. What we experience as color, sound, distance, time, and even objects themselves may be our mind's way of organizing something far more complex. This leads us into deeper questions about consciousness and existence. Is consciousness simply observing an external reality, or is it actively constructing the reality we experience? If our perception is a model created by the brain, then where exactly is the boundary between the world itself and the version of the world that exists inside our minds? These questions have been explored by philosophers, scientists, and thinkers for centuries, but modern ideas about perception and consciousness give us new ways to approach them. The goal isn't to claim that physical reality is fake, but to understand just how little of it we may actually experience directly. Because perhaps the strangest thing about reality isn't that we don't know what exists beyond it. It's that we may never experience reality exactly as it is.

metadata.title: Ralph Waldo Emerson: What If Everyone Alive is the Same Person, Just Wearing Different Faces?
metadata.description:
Ralph Waldo Emerson didn't just write essays, he made a claim that quietly rewired how an entire nation understood the self. 

In 1841, this former Unitarian minister, still reeling from the death of his young wife and his own crisis of faith, wrote something so radical that theologians of his time called it heresy: that there is no God "out there," no separate individual soul in here only one universal Oversoul, expressing itself through every person, every leaf, every stone, every stranger you'll ever meet.

In this video, we break down Emerson's Oversoul philosophy: what it actually claims, why he believed intuition not scripture, not reason  was the only real path to truth, and how his ideas quietly collided with Vedantic philosophy from the other side of the world centuries earlier.

We'll look at how modern ideas like Carl Jung's collective unconscious, quantum entanglement, and integrated information theory in consciousness research are edging toward the same conclusion Emerson reached two centuries ago.

If separateness really is an illusion if you, your enemy, and the stranger next to you on the train are all, underneath it all, the same wave rising off the same ocean, what does that mean for how you treat other people? What does it mean for who you actually are?


This is the story of the Oversoul, and why once you see it, you may never see yourself the same way again.



🔔 Subscribe for more deep dives into the philosophers, mystics and thinkers who challenged what it means to be human.


📚 Based on Ralph Waldo Emerson's 1841 essay "The Over-Soul"



⚠️ This video is for educational and philosophical discussion purposes. It presents Emerson's ideas and their historical/intellectual context and is not a substitute for reading the primary source.

🗣️ Dialogue on Consciousness and Reality: The Future of Scientific Understanding | Online Forum
📅 June 25, 2026
🎓 Hosted by Professors World Peace Academy – Los Angeles (PWPA-LA)


What if consciousness is not something the brain produces—but something more fundamental to reality itself? And if consciousness is fundamental, what does that mean for science, our understanding of the universe, and even our understanding of God?

On June 25, 2026, scholars from science, philosophy, and spirituality came together for an interdisciplinary dialogue exploring one of the deepest unanswered questions of our time: What is consciousness, and what is its place in reality?

The conversation explored:

• Is consciousness fundamental or emergent?
• Can science fully explain consciousness through the brain and physical matter?
• What evidence and research could advance the scientific study of consciousness?
• How might science, philosophy, and spirituality contribute to a deeper understanding of reality?

Rather than asking science and religion to stand apart, the dialogue asked whether bringing different perspectives together could open new possibilities for understanding consciousness and reality.

🎥 Watch the full recording and join the conversation.

metadata.title: On Becoming Human: Confucius and the Value of Philosophy
metadata.description:
This is the second lecture in a series of introductory videos on the character, values, and methods of philosophy. Its primary theme is the question of the value of doing and studying philosophy.

It focuses on the dilemma of saying something about the value of philosophy before one has advanced very far in the practice of philosophy, before suggesting that a rudimentary but compelling account of the value of philosophy can be found in the basic concepts of the philosophy of Confucius. The video then proceeds to examine the core contentions of Confucius's model of moral education, concluding with an application of this model to the value of the study of philosophy, situating it within the moral education of the human being.

0:00 Introduction: The Dilemma of Values
8:41 The Confucian Context
11:03 Li and the Confucian Moral Vision
19:32 Becoming Human
27:10 The Story of the Four Disciples

39:11 Conclusion: A Confucian Account of the Value of Philosophy

I owe great debts of gratitude to a number of creative commons resources, many of which I have extensively repurposed. 

The first and most obvious debt is to the Kirov’s performance of George Balanchine’s Serenade (The source for nearly all the ballet clips used in this video and for much of the music).

I am also especially indebted to the Griller Quintet and William Primrose's renditions of Mozart's Viola Quintets. metadata.title: The Coming of Age Symposium
metadata.description:
People are living longer across the world. But experiences of ageing are shaped by our environment, culture and society from the moment we’re born. Join us for a day of panel discussions exploring how greater longevity is playing out in societies today, and how they can adapt to ensure we all age better.
 
You’ll hear a range of perspectives on ageing, and engage with artists, campaigners and researchers involved in the ‘The Coming of Age’ exhibition, its accompanying book and beyond. The symposium will be chaired by Professor Pragya Agarwal.
 
Agenda:

Time: 11:00 – 11:15
Welcome and Curator’s Introduction
Shamita Sharmacharja, curator of ‘The Coming of Age’, opens the symposium.
 
Time: 11:15 – 12:45
Event Title: Ageing Better
We’re surrounded by different perspectives and stereotypes about getting older. 
But what does it mean to live longer in the UK today, and what needs to change so we can all age better? 
Researcher Martina Zimmermann, clinical academic Daniel Davis and The Centre for Ageing Better discuss ageism, the social determinants of health, and widening health and wealth gaps in later life.
 
Time: 14:00 – 14:30
Event title: Joyful Ageing
In this keynote, author and artist Karen Arthur reflects on joyful ageing in a world that often expects women to shrink and become invisible. She explores clothing as a way to support mental wellbeing, as well as thriving through menopause and the gift of growing older.
 
Time: 16:15 – 17:45
Event title: Ageing Inequities
Artist and academic Kit Green, disability researcher Tom Shakespeare and palliative medicine consultant Jamilla Hussain discuss how inequity shapes experiences of ageing for queer, disabled and racially minoritised communities. The conversation explores lived experiences of health inequity and the cumulative effects of ageing and discrimination.
 
Time: 17:45 – 18:00
Closing remarks
Chair Pragya Agarwal closes the symposium.
 
Need to know: 
 
This event will be live-transcribed, and British Sign Language interpreted.

metadata.title: The Forgotten Technique for Rewriting Your Mind | Carl jung Psyphology
metadata.description:
Carl Jung once did something no psychiatrist of his era would admit to: he sat down, closed his eyes, and deliberately talked to a voice inside his own unconscious mind. This documentary traces the real, historically documented method Jung built from that 1913 crisis, active imagination, and shows exactly why it worked, using Jung's own case notes, his encounter with the inner figure he called Philemon, and modern psychological research on self-distanced talk, parts-based therapy, and mental rehearsal. This isn't the recycled manifestation content built on Jung's name. It's the real Jungian technique behind the shadow, individuation, and synchronicity, simplified into a practice you can try tonight with nothing but a chair and ten honest minutes. If you've ever suspected that your loudest inner voice has been running your life without your permission, this Carl Jung psychology documentary finally explains why and what to do about it. Subscribe to Carl Jung Psyche for deeply researched psychology that never sacrifices accuracy for mystique.

metadata.title: The Moment Things Start Moving Again — Carl Jung
metadata.description:
Not every difficult stretch is a turning point, and not every turning point feels dramatic while it's happening. Carl Jung spent his career studying what actually distinguishes a genuine psychological shift from an ordinary rough patch — and his answer has less to do with external circumstances than most people assume.

This video looks at how Jung identified real turning points in his patients' lives: not by what was happening around them, but by what was shifting in their relationship to themselves. Drawing on his concepts of the persona, the shadow, and individuation, this is a look at what a genuine turning point actually involves, and how to recognize one in your own life without needing to wait for a dramatic external event.

What we explore:

The difference between an ordinary difficult period and a genuine psychological turning point, according to Jung's model. Why real turning points often involve discomfort and uncertainty rather than clarity. What Jung believed actually shifts, internally, when someone moves through one.

References & further reading:

Carl Jung — Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933); The Stages of Life (essay, in The Collected Works of C.G. Jung, Vol. 8); Psychology and Alchemy.

A note on accuracy: This video presents Jung's ideas in accessible language for a general audience. For the full depth and nuance of his work, the original texts above go much further than any single video can.

metadata.title: Brain, Mind, or Soul? What Neuroscience Can—and Can’t—Explain
metadata.description:
We know the brain and mind are connected. But does that prove the brain creates everything we experience as “us”?

In this episode of Blossoming Brains, Dr. Vicki Draeger explores the debate surrounding the brain, mind, consciousness, and soul—and why thoughtful scientists and physicians have reached very different conclusions from some of the same evidence.

Using a courtroom-style approach, we examine the arguments of neurosurgeons and researchers including Michael Egnor, Wilder Penfield, Eben Alexander, Pim van Lommel, and Bruce Greyson, along with the skeptical case represented by neurologist Steven Novella.

One of the central ideas is surprisingly simple: imagine the brain as a television. If damaging the television distorts the picture, does that prove the television created the signal? Or is the brain doing something more like receiving, processing, and expressing consciousness?

That analogy does not prove the existence of a soul—but it makes the real disagreement much easier to see.

🧠 Keep your brain growing for life:
👉 https://vickidraeger.com

What You’ll Learn
The difference between brain, mind, and soul
Why brain damage does not settle every philosophical question about consciousness
What Wilder Penfield reportedly observed during brain stimulation
Why personal agency remains such an intriguing part of the debate
How near-death experience research is used in arguments about consciousness
Why mainstream neuroscience rejects “we don’t know” as proof of a nonphysical explanation
Watch Next

Inside the Octopus Brain: Octopus Intelligence and a Truly Alien Mind

That episode takes the consciousness question in a completely different direction by looking at a nervous system that evolved very differently from our own.

If you enjoy thoughtful neuroscience explained without unnecessary jargon, like this video and subscribe to Blossoming Brains.

metadata.title: The Attribution of Meaning of Synchronicity in Psychotherapy by Jean-Francois Vezina, Psy.D
metadata.description:
Lecture at the 43rd International Human Science Research Conference by Jean-François Vézina, D.Psy 

The search for meaning represents a central dimension of human experience and holds a prominent place in the context of psychotherapy. This lecture present the results of a research exploring the process of meaning attribution during significant coincidences (SC) (sometimes referred to as synchronicities) experienced by psychotherapists and their patients within the therapeutic relationship.

Grounded in a qualitative, interpretive, and constructivist approach, this research aims to explore how these events are recognized, elaborated, and integrated into clinical work. Based on semi-structured interviews conducted with psychotherapists, this study examines the modalities of meaning co-construction, the subjective and relational effects of these experiences, and their transformative potential for both patient and therapist.

The results highlight the role of significant coincidences as emergences, moments of rupture and reorganization of meaning, that arise particularly during situations of clinical impasse or existential transition. Our findings also underscore the conditions under which meaning attribution can support emotional regulation and the therapeutic alliance during these emergences, while identifying the risks associated with defensive overinterpretation or a pathological rigidification of meaning.

We hope that this lecture will contribute to a better clinical understanding of significant coincidences in psychotherapy and offers conceptual and clinical guidelines aimed at fostering an integration of meaning that is at once creative, containing, and rigorous — in service of the therapeutic process rather than psychic defenses.

Keywords: significant coincidences, synchronicity, psychotherapy, meaning attribution, emotional regulation, individuation process.

PS: The research, on the supervision of Florence Vinit, Ph.D from UQUAM is availlible at the psychological departement of Shebrooke University

metadata.title: Jung's Synchronicity Explains What Spirituality Gets Wrong
metadata.description:
Carl Jung's synchronicity explains why manifestation works for some people and not others. In 1952 Jung published a paper the scientific community laughed at — and it explains the law of attraction better than the law of attraction ever has.

Synchronicity is the meaningful coincidence of an outer event with your inner state, with no causal connection between them. In plain English: the outer world responds to the inner world. This video breaks down the five principles Carl Jung actually discovered, and why the manifestation world keeps getting them wrong.

Most manifestation advice fails because it treats reality like a vending machine. Jung's thirty years of clinical observation point somewhere else entirely — synchronicity clusters when your conscious and unconscious mind are aligned. Affirm abundance on the surface while scarcity runs underneath, and the signal dies. That one insight from Jungian psychology explains almost every inconsistent result you have ever had.

Jung spent his life trying to show us one thing: the inner world and the outer world aren't separate. They're two faces of the same reality — and synchronicity is the bridge you can watch unfold in your own life.
If Jungian psychology, manifestation and the psychology of the unconscious are your thing, subscribe — this channel goes deeper than surface-level spirituality.

metadata.title: TRUE DEVOTION EXPECTS NOTHING | Devendra Mohan Satsang | 12.07.2026

@bhaiyajisatsang 

This is an AI-translated English voice version of the original Hindi Satsang, published with permission.

--------------------------------------------------

We pray. We meditate. We attend Satsang. We seek the presence of the Guru.

But somewhere within us, a question may remain:

Why is my suffering still there?
Why are my wishes not being fulfilled?
Why is God not giving me what I ask for?

In this Satsang, Devendra Mohan invites us to look deeply at what we call devotion.

If our relationship with God is based on requests, expectations and the hope of receiving something in return, is it really devotion – or has it quietly become a transaction?

True Bhakti is not about convincing God to arrange life according to our wishes. It is about love, trust and surrender without conditions.

🪷 IN THIS SATSANG, YOU WILL UNDERSTAND:

• The difference between true devotion and a spiritual transaction
• Why constantly asking God to fulfil our wishes can keep us from understanding Bhakti
• How expectations influence our relationship with God and the Guru
• Why worldly possessions and pleasures cannot give us what we truly seek
• What surrender really means on the spiritual path
• Why devotion begins to change when we stop asking, “What will I get?”

✨ YOU WILL ALSO DISCOVER:

• Why surrender does not mean weakness or giving up
• How our desire to control outcomes can enter even our spiritual practice
• Why telling an all-knowing God what He should do for us creates a contradiction
• How meditation can become an offering instead of another goal to achieve
• What it means to give your time to the Divine without expecting anything in return
• Why trust becomes possible when our demands begin to fall away

💙 THIS SATSANG IS FOR YOU IF...

• you sometimes wonder why your prayers seem unanswered
• you find yourself asking God or the Guru to change circumstances in your life
• you want to understand the deeper meaning of Bhakti
• surrender sounds beautiful to you but is difficult to practise
• meditation sometimes feels like something you need to accomplish
• you want your spiritual relationship to be based more on love than expectation

🪷 REMEMBER...

Devotion is not:

“I give you my prayers, and you give me what I want.”

True devotion begins when the transaction ends.

When asking becomes trusting.
When expectation becomes surrender.
When meditation is no longer something we perform to achieve a result, but time we simply offer to the Divine.

👉 TAKE A MOMENT TO REFLECT:

If none of my wishes were fulfilled, would my love and devotion remain the same?

Perhaps that question brings us closer to understanding what Bhakti truly means.

metadata.title: Carl Jung: Synchronicities and the Meaningful Patterns of Life
metadata.description:
Have you ever had a coincidence feel too specific to be nothing — a thought followed almost immediately by the exact event you were thinking about? Carl Jung took moments like this seriously enough to build a real, if genuinely contested, theory around them.

This video explores what Jung actually meant by synchronicity: a meaningful coincidence between an inner psychological state and an outer event, connected by significance rather than cause and effect. It covers where the idea came from, the real, documented cases Jung built it on, and why it remains one of the most debated parts of his work among psychologists today.

What we explore:

Jung's precise definition of synchronicity, and how it differs from the popular, watered-down version of the term. The real clinical cases that led Jung to develop the theory. Why synchronicity remains scientifically contested, and what a fair, balanced view of the idea actually looks like.

References & further reading:

Carl Jung — Synchronicity: An Acausal Connecting Principle; Memories, Dreams, Reflections; Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933).

A note on accuracy: This video presents Jung's ideas as interpretive theory, not settled science. Synchronicity in particular remains genuinely debated among psychologists and philosophers of science. For the full depth of Jung's work, the original texts above go much further than any single video can.

Context:- We can study the brain with extraordinary precision. We can measure thoughts, decode decisions, and even map the mechanisms behind self-awareness. But does understanding the brain necessarily mean understanding ourselves?

At University College London (UCL), Acharya Prashant is in conversation with cognitive neuroscientist Prof. Stephen Fleming for a wide-ranging dialogue on self-knowledge, consciousness, metacognition, the brain, the mind, memory, free will, ego, psychological suffering, and the nature of awareness. As the conversation unfolds, it engages with the work of Daniel Dennett, Roger Sperry, Michael Gazzaniga, Donald Hoffman, Roger Penrose, Stuart Hameroff, the Buddha, Nagarjuna, and Adi Shankaracharya, examining where neuroscience and philosophy converge, and where they continue to ask fundamentally different questions.

Through an extended dialogue and audience Q&A, the conversation explores why neuroscience, philosophy, and education remain incomplete without self-knowledge, and whether understanding the brain alone can ever resolve the deeper questions of consciousness, suffering, and the human condition.  

Key Themes:
- Consciousness through the lens of neuroscience and Vedanta

Last Minute Lecture is a student-run project and is currently funded entirely by students who believe educational resources should remain free and accessible. If Last Minute Lecture has helped you study, please consider supporting the project.

All chapters are now available for free on our new platform:
https://lastminutelecture.com

📚 Consciousness encompasses the ongoing awareness of our internal states and external surroundings, operating through dual processing pathways where conscious and unconscious mental activity occurs simultaneously. The human sleep-wake cycle is anchored to circadian rhythms, a biological clock regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus responding to light cues and controlling melatonin secretion from the pineal gland. Sleep progresses through five distinct stages in approximately 90-minute cycles, beginning with relaxed wakefulness characterized by alpha wave activity, progressing through transitional stage one with hypnagogic hallucinations, stage two marked by sleep spindles, stages three and four featuring deep slow-wave delta activity, and finally REM sleep where rapid eye movements accompany vivid dreams despite motor system paralysis. Sleep serves critical adaptive functions including memory consolidation, neural tissue restoration, facilitation of creative problem-solving, and hormonal regulation supporting physical growth, while chronic sleep deprivation impairs cognitive function, weakens immunity, and increases accident risk. Sleep disorders such as insomnia, narcolepsy with sudden REM intrusions, sleep apnea involving breathing cessation, and night terrors during deep sleep represent common disruptions to healthy rest patterns. Dreams predominantly occur during REM sleep and involve ordinary scenarios often colored by negative emotional content; competing theoretical frameworks explain dreams as wish-fulfillment mechanisms with unconscious wish content disguised as manifest storylines, as memory consolidation processes, as preservation of neural pathways through brain stimulation, as the brain's synthesis of random neural activity, or as reflections of cognitive developmental level. Hypnosis functions as a social interaction involving suggestion where effectiveness depends on individual susceptibility rather than practitioner skill, with theoretical explanations ranging from social role enactment to dissociated consciousness with differential awareness across mental systems. Psychoactive drugs alter consciousness by modifying synaptic neural transmission, with repeated use producing tolerance necessitating escalated doses and generating potential withdrawal and addiction cycles. Drug categories include depressants reducing neural activity through alcohol and opiates, stimulants elevating arousal via caffeine and cocaine, and hallucinogens distorting perception through LSD and THC, with usage patterns influenced by interacting biological predispositions, psychological needs including stress relief and meaning-seeking, and sociocultural factors such as peer influence and normative expectations.

Original video (Hindi):

@bhaiyajisatsang 

This is an AI-translated English voice version of the original Hindi Satsang, published with permission.

--------------------------------------------------

We spend so much of our lives trying to change what is happening around us.

We want other people to understand us.
We want our families to behave the way we think they should.
We want recognition for what we do.
We want situations to unfold according to our plans.
And even in spirituality, we may find ourselves asking God or the Guru to fulfil our wishes.

But what if the real obstacle to peace is not the world around us?

What if it is the “I” within us that constantly wants to control, achieve, receive and be acknowledged?

In this Satsang, Devendra Mohan explores the subtle role of ego in our spiritual journey and invites us to look honestly at our expectations — from life, from other people, from the Guru and even from God.

True spirituality does not begin when the world finally behaves according to our wishes.

It begins when we stop demanding that it does.

🪷 IN THIS SATSANG, YOU WILL UNDERSTAND:

• Why the “I” can become one of the greatest obstacles on the spiritual path
• How our desire for recognition, status and control influences our inner state
• Why constantly trying to change other people creates suffering
• The difference between wanting something from God and truly surrendering to God
• Why meditation is not another achievement, but an act of surrender
• How expectations can quietly disturb our relationships and our peace

✨ YOU WILL ALSO DISCOVER:

• Why God is not something we need to search for outside ourselves
• How letting go of control can transform difficult situations
• Why surrender does not mean giving up, but trusting more deeply
• How to stop making your happiness dependent on other people's opinions
• Why criticism only has as much power over you as you give it
• How learning to smile in the face of judgement can create an extraordinary inner freedom
• Why gratitude can change the way we experience both spirituality and everyday life

💙 THIS SATSANG IS FOR YOU IF...

• you often feel responsible for fixing everything around you
• you struggle when people do not behave the way you expect
• criticism or other people's opinions easily disturb your peace
• you find it difficult to let go of control
• you want to understand surrender beyond the idea of simply “giving up”
• you want spirituality to become something you live rather than something you only practise

🪷 REMEMBER...

Inner peace does not begin when everyone finally understands you.

It does not begin when your family changes.

It does not begin when nobody criticises you anymore.

And it does not begin when life finally follows your plans.

Peace begins when the need to control everything slowly becomes trust.

When expectation becomes acceptance.

When “I want” becomes “I surrender.”

And perhaps one of the deepest questions we can ask ourselves is:

“How much of my suffering comes from what is actually happening — and how much comes from my expectation that it should be different?”

Take some time with this Satsang.

Listen without trying to find another person who needs to hear it.

Listen for the places within yourself where the “I” still wants to control, prove, demand or be recognised.

Sometimes the greatest obstacle between us and peace is not the world.

It is the part of us that insists the world must be different before we allow ourselves to be at peace.

But how much of life is actually under our control?

metadata.title: She was dead for two weeks. On Earth, only minutes passed.
metadata.description:
She was dead for two weeks. On Earth, only minutes passed.

In this episode of Catskill Liminal Walk, I take the story of Elizabeth Krohn - a Houston mother struck by lightning on her way to Shabbat services - and trace what happened in the space between her death and her return. The strike, the clinical death, the out-of-body experience, and the world she woke up in: a garden where a voice she recognized as her grandfather's told her she had a choice.

What she was shown there - the two weeks that felt like minutes, the foreknowledge of a daughter not yet conceived, the glimpse of reincarnation - raises the biggest questions: what is consciousness, what happens when we die, and what do accounts like this tell us about the nature of existence?

I also draw a line to Betty Andreasson's experience, comparing how two very different traumas - a lightning strike and an abduction - can open into similar spiritual encounters.

This is a documented and detailed account, cowritten with Jeff Kripal, a professor of comparative religion at Rice University.

📖 The book behind this story: "Changed in a Flash: One Woman's Near-Death Experience and Why a Scholar Thinks It Empowers Us All," Elizabeth G. Krohn and Jeffrey J. Kripal (2018)

metadata.title: Epictetus on What's Up to You — and What Isn'
metadata.description:
The Handbook of Epictetus — known in Greek as the Encheiridion — is one of the most widely read texts in Stoicism. In this video I work through several of its chapters and share what I took from each one.

Epictetus never wrote a word of it. The Handbook was assembled by Flavius Arrian, a student of his, from notes taken during the lectures.
And the title is worth pausing on: encheiridion means something carried in the hand — a handbook — but it also means a dagger, the short blade a Roman soldier kept at his belt. This was never a book meant for study. It was a book meant to be carried and drawn when you needed it.

The starting point is the division that opens the work. There are things that depend on us — our judgments, desires, choices and actions — and things that don't: the body, reputation, money, other people's opinions. Confusing the two, Epictetus argues, is the source of most human suffering. When we place our happiness in what we don't control, we become hostage to it.

In chapter 5, he makes the claim the whole book rests on: it isn't things that disturb people, but the opinions they form about them. He uses death as his example, and Socrates as his proof — if death were terrible by nature, it would have seemed terrible to Socrates too. The chapter also traces a progression: from blaming others, to blaming yourself, to blaming no one at all.

Chapter 8 contains one of the harshest lines in the book: don't wish for things to happen as you want them to — wish for them to happen as they do happen. I explain why this is neither resignation nor passivity.

Chapter 17 gives us the image of the theatre. We're handed a role we didn't choose, and what's up to us is to play it well. Chapter 33 gathers practical guidance on conduct: speak less, don't judge others, don't chase approval, keep some things about your own life to yourself.

The video also looks at the urge to be seen, and the weight other people's opinions take on in the life of someone who depends on them — an old problem that social media has only made more visible.

Chapters discussed: 1, 5, 8, 17 and 33.

Where to read it

The Handbook is short — a couple of hours, start to finish — and I'd recommend reading the whole thing rather than taking my word for any of it. In English, Robin Hard's translation for Oxford World's Classics is the standard modern choice, and it comes bundled with the Discourses. Elizabeth Carter's 18th-century translation is in the public domain and free to read online through Project Gutenberg and the MIT Internet Classics Archive. Anthony Long's How to Be Free (Princeton) is another good option, with the Greek printed alongside.

One word of warning: Sharon Lebell's The Art of Living is often shelved with these, but it's a loose modern interpretation rather than a translation. Worth knowing before you buy.

If you've ever spent days chewing over a single piece of criticism, or tried to control something that was never in your hands, leave a comment — I read all of them.

metadata.title: Neuroscience, Synchronicities, & the Evidence for a Playful Universe — Dr. Marjorie Woollacott
metadata.description:
In this episode, Niall speaks with Dr. Marjorie Woollacott, Professor Emerita of Neuroscience at the University of Oregon and former President of the Academy for the Advancement of Postmaterialist Sciences. 

After more than 30 years of NIH-funded research on motor control, balance, and rehabilitation, a profound meditation experience led her to question her understanding of consciousness and reality.

In this conversation, they explore:

— Why Dr. Woollacott's research with nonverbal autistic children is raising questions about telepathic abilities

— How the brain may act as a filter that limits our perception of a much larger reality

— The scientific evidence for reincarnation from researchers including Ian Stevenson and Jim Tucker

— What synchronicities may reveal about the interconnected nature of consciousness


— Why pursuing a parallel line of research allowed Dr. Woollacott to study consciousness while building her academic career

You can learn more about Dr. Woollacott's work at https://marjoriewoollacott.com.

---

Marjorie Woollacott, Ph.D., is an Emeritus Professor of Human Physiology at the University of Oregon and a renowned neuroscientist specializing in human movement, attention, meditation, and consciousness. She has received more than $7.2 million in research funding and has conducted research in child development, aging, rehabilitation, meditation, tai chi, balance, and attentional abilities. Woollacott has published over 200 scientific articles and authored or co-edited eight books, including the widely used textbook Motor Control: Translating Research into Clinical Practice. She is Research Director of the International Association of Near-Death Studies and President of the Academy for the Advancement of Postmaterialist Sciences. Her book Infinite Awareness explores the relationship between neuroscience, consciousness, and spiritual experiences, reflecting her work at the intersection of scientific research and questions about the nature of the mind.

In this fascinating Carl Jung-inspired lecture, you'll explore the profound concept of synchronicity—one of Jung's most intriguing and thought-provoking ideas. According to Jung, some events are connected not by cause and effect, but by meaning. Jung believed that the human psyche is deeply connected to symbolic patterns that often appear through dreams, unexpected encounters, and seemingly impossible coincidences. Whether synchronicity reflects the hidden structure of reality or simply the remarkable way the mind creates meaning, Jung's theory invites us to look beyond appearances and develop a deeper relationship with ourselves and the world around us.

metadata.title: The Mind Is the Body's Idea — Spinoza's Theory of Love (Lecture 2)
metadata.description:
Lecture 2 of "Introduction to Spinoza and his Theory of Love."

Watch the full lecture series:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLJLzNR1DlSnk

Presented by Ergo, a nonprofit that publishes structured philosophical lectures online, free to anyone. https://ergo.org

About this lecture

Why do we feel so certain that we need free will? And what holds a body together from one moment to the next? In this lecture, Noa Lahav Ayalon works through Spinoza's radical alternative to Descartes' dualism, showing how the mind is not a separate substance but the idea of the body. She traces how Cartesian thinking still shapes our everyday assumptions before turning to Spinoza's physical digression: the claim that what keeps a body alive is a specific proportion of motion and rest among its parts, actively resisting dissipation. From there, the lecture builds toward Spinoza's three kinds of knowledge (imagination, reason, and intuition), and explains how adequate and inadequate ideas work in practice. The session closes with conatus, the drive every thing has to persevere in its own being, setting the stage for the next lecture on how this drive manifests in our emotional lives.

About this course

In this four-lecture course, Noa Lahav Ayalon traces Spinoza's philosophy from its metaphysical foundations to his vision of love and human flourishing. Beginning with the foundational claim that God and nature are one, Ayalon explores conatus, the striving by which every being perseveres in existence, and asks what becomes of free will if we are parts of nature. The course then examines desire and emotion, arguing that we define ourselves by what we love, and culminates in Spinoza's three kinds of love, where the intellectual love of God offers salvation. Spinoza refused to publish his masterwork, Ethics, during his lifetime for fear of persecution, but his thinking went on to hold vast influence in philosophy (Hegel, Nietzsche), science (Einstein, Schrödinger), and the arts (Goethe, Borges, George Eliot).No prior background in philosophy is required.

About Noa Lahav Ayalon

Noa Lahav Ayalon is a lecturer of philosophy in the Department of Humanities and Arts at the Technion, Israel Institute of Technology. She was previously a Postdoctoral Fellow in Philosophy at Harvard University and a Rothschild Fellow. Her research focuses on early modern philosophy, particularly Spinoza's metaphysics, affect theory, and ethics, and the intersection of philosophy and science.

metadata.title: Vladislav Andreev - Psychonaut
metadata.description:
What if a psychedelic experience is only the beginning?

In this episode of The Oliver Schirach Show, I sit down with Vladislav (Vlad) Andreev, neuroscience-based coach, public educator and founder of O!Sapiens, for a deep conversation about psychedelics, neuroscience, trauma, mental health, neuroplasticity and personal transformation.

Vlad takes us through his journey from corporate burnout to becoming a public educator exploring the therapeutic potential of psychedelics. From there, the conversation opens into a deeper exploration of what psychedelics can reveal about the brain, the unconscious mind, and ourselves — and why what happens after the experience may be just as important as the experience itself.

We explore the neuroplasticity window and the opportunity it creates for change, before moving into psychedelic integration, difficult trips, confronting our inner “demons,” and the ways trauma — including cultural and intergenerational trauma — can shape our identity and the stories we tell ourselves.

This naturally leads us beyond psychedelics and into a bigger conversation about mental health, wellbeing and longevity. We talk about sleep, movement, nutrition, stress, relationships, curiosity, purpose and inflammation — and how these seemingly simple pieces can shape the way we experience life.

At the heart of the conversation is one bigger question:
How much of who we are is actually us — and how much was programmed into us by our family, culture and environment?

Together, we question old patterns, explore consciousness and personal responsibility, and look at how profound experiences can become real, lasting changes in everyday life.

Ultimately, this is a Hero’s Journey — from losing yourself, through confronting what lies beneath the surface, to discovering new possibilities for who you can become.
This episode is for curious minds, psychonauts, spiritual seekers, and anyone interested in consciousness, personal growth, neuroscience and the potential of psychedelics to transform our relationship with ourselves.

We discuss:
 • Psychedelics & neuroscience

What is the origin of consciousness, and why do humans experience a subjective inner world and question their own existence?

In this fascinating documentary from The Origin Files, we explore the mystery of consciousness, the hard problem of consciousness, the evolution of life, and the controversial philosophical idea of panpsychism.

From the chemistry of ancient Earth and the emergence of early life to the evolution of increasingly complex nervous systems and human cognitive abilities, this journey examines different scientific and philosophical perspectives on one of the deepest questions we can ask: How did conscious experience emerge?

Could conscious experience arise from the complex activity of the brain, or might there be a deeper relationship between consciousness and the fundamental nature of reality? Science has not yet reached a definitive answer, and ideas such as panpsychism remain subjects of philosophical debate.

Explore the fascinating intersection of consciousness, the human mind, neuroscience, evolution, philosophy, life, and the universe.

Watch until the end and share your thoughts: Where do you think consciousness comes from?

Tausende Menschen aus dem Bonner Umfeld nahmen in diesen Jahren in Kleingruppen an den 8-Wochen-MBSR-Kursen teil, die von Angelika und ihren Kolleginnen durchgeführt wurden.

metadata.title: Carl Jung on the Psychological Signs of Real Progress
metadata.description:
Not every improvement announces itself. Carl Jung identified specific internal shifts that tend to mark genuine psychological progress — distinct from simply feeling good in the moment, or from circumstances happening to improve on their own.

This video walks through the concrete signs Jung associated with real movement toward wholeness: changes in how a person relates to conflict, to their own reactions, and to parts of themselves they used to avoid. Rather than a vague sense of "things are looking up," this is a specific, checkable framework for recognizing when internal change is actually taking place.

What we explore:

The specific psychological markers Jung associated with genuine progress, as distinct from temporary mood improvement. How a person's relationship to their own reactions changes as real integration takes place. Why these signs are often internal and easy to miss, rather than dramatic or externally visible.

References & further reading:

Carl Jung — Psychology and Alchemy (on individuation and transformation); Modern Man in Search of a Soul (1933); Two Essays on Analytical Psychology.

A note on accuracy: This video presents Jung's ideas in accessible language for a general audience. For the full depth and nuance of his work, the original texts above go much further than any single video can.

metadata.title: Qualia and Hard Problem of Consciousness by The Imaginary Guy Himself FinnO4 | WTA | Lecture 2
metadata.description:
In Part 2 of our Consciousness series, we dive into one of the deepest and most fascinating questions in philosophy of mind and consciousness studies: Why does subjective experience exist at all?

What does it actually feel like to see a colour, hear music, experience pain, remember a moment, or simply be aware of yourself? These first-person experiences are often referred to as Qualia — the subjective, experiential qualities of conscious experience.

From here, we encounter David Chalmers’ Hard Problem of Consciousness: even if neuroscience can explain how the brain processes information, why do those physical processes produce a subjective experience in the first place? Why isn't the brain simply processing information without there being an inner experience?

In this video, we explore the difference between explaining the functions and mechanisms of the brain and explaining the existence of conscious experience itself. We also look at questions surrounding physicalism, the explanatory gap, subjective experience, and the possibility that consciousness may require a deeper explanation than conventional neuroscience currently provides.





This is not about giving a final answer—it is about understanding the problem clearly and exploring why consciousness remains one of the greatest mysteries in science and philosophy.

Witness the Anomalous (WTA) — exploring consciousness, anomalous phenomena, parapsychology, metaphysics, and the unexplained.

metadata.title: 2.9 Locating the Mind — Ms. Caitlin Mace
metadata.description:
What exactly does it mean to think? Where are memories stored? And can studying the brain really tell us how the mind works?

This episode features Caitlin Mace, a graduate student at the University of Pittsburgh whose research focuses on the philosophy of neuroscience. She previously earned her master’s degree in philosophy from California State University, Long Beach.

In this episode, Mace explores the relationship between philosophy and neuroscience, asking what scientists can—and cannot—learn by breaking the brain into its component parts. She discusses reductionism, mental representation, optogenetics, and the challenge of determining where memories are physically stored. She also examines false memories, the surprising ways our recollections change over time, and whether memory might extend beyond the brain itself.

Dialexicon is a free podcast dedicated to promoting philosophical education and deep reflection. We invite scholars from around the globe to discuss philosophy in the context of contemporary social issues—all at an easy-to-understand and digestible level.

metadata.title: The Theology of Spinoza
metadata.description:
Is God the same as the universe? Is everything that exists within God, or does God transcend what we can observe? Whether understood as an atheist, a pantheist, or a panentheist, Spinoza has influenced philosophy and theology from the dawn of the Enlightenment to this day. 

A forerunner of the Enlightenment, Baruch Spinoza was born in the multi-cultural Dutch Republic of the 17th century, to Jewish parents who had from the Portuguese Inquisition. In his philosophical explorations, Spinoza rejected Biblical portraits of God maintained in Judaism and Christianity. Taking the ontological argument for God (famously developed by Descartes) even further, Spinoza stated “whatever is, is in God” — developing a metaphysics in which God is identical with the universe. Spinoza summarized this idea with the phrase “Deus sive Natura” (God or Nature), which some readers have taken as an equation of God and Nature (pantheism) or a replacement of the idea of God with Nature (atheism).  

In this live lecture, John Hamer of Toronto Centre Place looks at the development of Spinoza’s theology within its historical and cultural context. Did Spinoza reject religion, or was he trying to separate genuine knowledge of God from superstition and scriptural literalism? Why did he provoke such strong reactions in both Jewish and Christian circles? 

Join the livestream to participate in the discussion and to ask questions of our lecturer during the Q&A.

This lecture is part of our series exploring Christianity and the Bible from an academic perspective through history, mythology, archaeology, theology, and biblical studies. In this presentation we focus on Baruch Spinoza, the development of his theology, pantheism, panintheism, and the beginnings of the Enlightenment.

metadata.title: Chapter 6 | The Cosmic Hierarchy
metadata.description:
Chapter 6 turns to the structure at the center of Ḥamza ibn ʿAlī’s system: the five principal ḥudūd beneath al-Ḥākim.

The hierarchy identifies historical members of the early Druze daʿwa with eternal cosmic ranks:

Ḥamza ibn ʿAlī — Universal Intellect, al-ʿAql al-Kullī
Ismāʿīl al-Tamīmī — Universal Soul, al-Nafs al-Kulliyya
Muḥammad ibn Wahb al-Qurashī — the Word, al-Kalima
Salāma ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Samurrī — the Precedent, al-Sābiq
Bahāʾ al-Dīn al-Muqtanā — the Follower, al-Tālī

The surviving manuscript tradition also preserves appointment documents attributed to Ḥamza for several of these men. That gives us unusually concrete historical evidence for organization inside the daʿwa.

But it creates an important distinction.

A document can help establish that Ḥamza appointed a man to a religious office. It does not, by itself, establish that the same man is the earthly appearance of an eternal metaphysical principle.

The chapter therefore separates category from identification.

Universal Intellect and Universal Soul did not begin with Ḥamza. Earlier Ismāʿīlī philosophers such as Abū Yaʿqūb al-Sijistānī had already developed an ordered cosmology of Intellect and Soul.

The inherited philosophy gives us the categories.

The additional claim is that Ḥamza is the Universal Intellect, al-Tamīmī the Universal Soul, and the other members of the daʿwa the remaining cosmic ranks.

Druze sacred history then extends those same ḥudūd backward through earlier religious ages. In the age of Muḥammad, the five ranks are associated with Salmān al-Fārisī, al-Miqdād, Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and al-Najāshī.

The hierarchy therefore becomes more than an organization in eleventh-century Cairo. It becomes a key for rereading sacred history.

The chapter then tests the same method against the Christian cycle. Druze tradition distinguishes a visible Jesus from a higher true Christ, while Qurʾān 4:157 presents “the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary” as a single referent and denies that he was killed or crucified.

That does not by itself prove an esoteric interpretation false. But it raises the same evidentiary question:

Where does the additional identification come from?

If the authority of the hidden hierarchy is used to establish the identities, while those identities are then used to establish the hierarchy’s authority, the investigation reaches its central problem.

Internal coherence is not the same as independent verification.

Chapter 7 asks what, if anything, independently carries us from belief in one necessary transcendent God to these particular historical and cosmic identifications.

metadata.title: Jack Lindsey and Patrick Butlin, "What Does Claude’s J-Space Tell Us About Consciousness?"
metadata.channel: NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy
metadata.uploader: NYU Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy
metadata.description:
About the Event

Anthropic’s recent paper on a global workspace in language models identifies a set of internal representations in Claude — the “J-space” — that appear to perform some of the functions associated with global workspace theories of consciousness. How far should we take this finding? In this webinar, Anthropic’s Jack Lindsey, who led this research project, and Eleos’s Patrick Butlin, who co-authored an external commentary, will discuss what the J-space does and does not reveal about LLM minds. The conversation will explore the possibility of a global workspace in LLMs, the possibility of consciousness in LLMs, and the broader value of using theories of consciousness to study AI cognition and behavior. There will be time for questions and comments from the audience as well.

About the Speakers

Jack Lindsey leads the Model Psychology team at Anthropic. His team investigates the internal basis of high-level cognition in language models and applies this research to monitor models’ motivations as part of safety evaluations, as well as to inform training strategies that shape their character. Previously, Jack completed a Ph.D. at Columbia’s Center for Theoretical Neuroscience, where he studied the neural basis of learning and memory. Jack holds an M.S. in computer science and a B.S. in mathematics from Stanford University.

Patrick Butlin is a philosopher of mind and cognitive science and Senior Research Lead at Eleos AI Research. His work focuses on the mental capacities and attributes that could ground moral status in AI, such as consciousness and agency. He was previously a researcher at the University of Oxford, first at the Future of Humanity Institute and then the Global Priorities Institute.

This event is co-sponsored by the NYU Center for Mind, Brain, and Consciousness.

metadata.title: Your BRAIN is LYING to YOU
metadata.description:
What if everything you remember isn't actually real? A neuroscientist explains how your brain constantly confabulates and deceives you about reality itself.

0:00 The Confabulous Brain Intro
1:03 Philosophy of Reality & The Matrix
4:18 Mrs. B's Case of Confabulation
6:46 Brain Damage & Confabulation Syndrome
8:11 True vs False Memory in the Brain
9:32 Study on Reality Recognition
12:34 Prefrontal Cortex & Fantasy vs Reality
14:00 Electrical Signals & Belief

Ever wonder if your memories are accurate or if your brain is playing tricks on you? In this eye-opening talk, neuroscientist Matthew Collins explores the fascinating concept of the "confabulous brain"—how our minds constantly construct false memories and distort reality without us even knowing it. Drawing parallels to The Matrix and classical philosophy from Descartes, Collins reveals the unsettling truth: you can't always trust your own senses or memories. If you can't tell the difference between what's real and what your brain imagined, how do you know anything is real at all? This talk challenges everything you think you know about consciousness, perception, and the nature of reality itself.

metadata.title: Mental Health Case Files Ep. 4 | Anxiety Disorders #trainingvideo  #mentalhealth  #anxiety
metadata.description:
Emeka is a 24-year-old university student who appears to be doing everything right. He studies hard, attends his lectures, and wants to succeed. But behind the books and busy university life, he is fighting a battle that nobody can see.

Every day, Emeka is overwhelmed by excessive worry. His heart races, his stomach hurts, he struggles to concentrate, and his mind is constantly filled with "what if?" thoughts.

As the anxiety gets worse, Emeka begins avoiding class discussions and social activities. He struggles to sleep, his grades start falling, and even simple tasks become overwhelming. Then, without warning, he experiences a terrifying episode of intense fear, dizziness, racing heartbeat, and difficulty breathing.

Some people tell him to "calm down." Others think he is being dramatic or that it is "all in his mind." But Emeka eventually learns an important lesson: anxiety is real, and anxiety disorders are treatable.

This emotional and educational story explores the warning signs of anxiety disorders, panic attacks, excessive worry, avoidance, physical symptoms, sleep problems, and the importance of early professional support.

Sometimes, one person noticing... one person listening... and one person taking someone's struggle seriously can become the beginning of recovery.

metadata.title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra - Illustrated Audiobook for Focused Reading (Part 1/2)
metadata.description:
Friedrich Nietzsche (1883-1885)
The book follows the prophet Zarathustra as he descends from his mountain solitude to teach humanity about the arrival of the Superman and the necessity of self-overcoming. Through a series of poetic discourses and parables, it critiques traditional morality and religion while advocating for the affirmation of life and the creation of new values.

Part 1 of 2. An illustrated audiobook of the public-domain classic: the narration is synced word by word with the on-screen text, classic artwork illustrates the scenes. Speed-reading format suitable for ADHD.

metadata.title: Synchronicity as Inner Maps: Hidden Keys in Daily Life
metadata.description:
ChuChai invites you to slow your gaze and listen for the hidden keys woven through daily life. Synchronicity is framed as an inner map, a language written in signs we ordinarily overlook. The narration asks not for proof but for practice: to notice patterns, to test intentions, to read life with curiosity rather than need for certainty. This episode is an invitation to co-create meaning with the world, and to see every small symbol as a doorway toward deeper self-understanding. The Life Saga app awaits your own mapping of meaning.

What if the small coincidences—the sign on a wall, the song that repeats, the moment of recognition—are not random, but intentional nudges toward growth? What if your inner compass is learning to read a language the world already speaks? The episode does not claim to prove anything; it asks you to listen, to pause, to act with awareness, and to discover how you become the one who finds the key.

"The map is inside you, waiting to be read."
